title: Millridge · A Call at Night
sceneText:
Gregor asked nothing at all and went to saddle up.

But while he was saddling he looked at you. Once, and then he bent to the girth.

The kitchen light was still on as you went out. Martha stood in the doorway with something in her hands and watched you mount. She said nothing either.

An hour’s ride. There is no moon, and Gregor hung you a lantern.

What you think about on the road is this: by tomorrow morning this ride will be all over the valley. Nobody here goes out at night. When one household’s horse goes out after dark, the whole village knows by the next day.

And towards Millridge, particularly.

The porter at Millridge is not yet in bed. He sees you and shows no surprise either.

Henk is in the study in house clothes, with the fire well up. He sees you come in, puts down what is in his hand and stands.

“Late,” he says.

There is no surprise on his face.

He pours two glasses, sets one in front of you, then sits back with his hands folded across his front and waits for you to speak.

You speak.

He hears you out and nods, with no expression at all.

“It has not been an easy year at Maplegate,” he says. “Ludwig comes home for three days a year, and the other three hundred and sixty-two rest on the steward. Hartmann carried it eight years. You have carried it a month.”

He takes a drink.

“Go on. What do you need.”

variants.short_of_trust:
He hears you out, and one eyebrow moves.

Then he smiles. It is not the smile he usually has. The usual one is for you; this one is for himself.

He puts the glass down and leans back in the chair.

“I have had you to dinner once, asked you to a hunt once, and put a proposal to you once about carrying timber,” he says. “That last one you have still not answered.”

“I am not keeping accounts,” he says. “I am saying that you and I are not yet on those terms.”

He stands, goes to the desk, takes something out of a drawer and sets it in front of you.

One guldmark.

“Take it,” he says. “Get something for the horse on the road.”

He does not sit down again.

“Mind yourself riding back,” he says. “That road is poor in autumn.”

The porter sees you out. Through all of it Henk does not say another word.

On the way home you think of Martha standing in the kitchen doorway, watching you mount.

effects.logEntry: In the study at Millridge you said you needed a good deal.

choices.resultText:
He did not make you say it twice.

“Right,” he says, and calls out through the door. Somebody answers.

For the next quarter of an hour the Millridge men are loading the cart. Grain, timber, a small bag of money absurdly heavy for its size. You stand in the yard and watch them load. One of them comes over to ask what weight the boards will take, and you cannot tell him, so he goes and looks himself.

Henk comes out with a coat over his shoulders and stands beside you.

“Enough for the winter,” he says. “Keep what is over; it will do for the spring sowing as well.”

You say the amount is too much.

“Neighbours,” he says.

He watches the cart, not you.

“There will come a time when you are of use to me.”

That is all of it. He does not say when, and he does not say what, and he does not ask you to agree to anything.

You stand together and watch them finish loading. He claps you on the shoulder and says to mind the road.

You ride home slowly. The cart is heavy, the horse goes slowly, the lantern swings.

You agreed to nothing.

But what you are carrying home is the kind of thing that, once accepted, cannot be accounted for.

effects.logEntry: At Millridge you asked for cash.

choices.resultText:
“Money is easy,” he says.

He has a cloth bag brought in, counts it through in front of you, and pushes it across.

The amount is exactly the amount you needed. You never named a figure.

“Call it a loan from me,” he says. “Repay it whenever.”

He is smiling when he says whenever.

You put the bag in an inside pocket. It is heavier than you expected.

effects.logEntry: At Millridge you asked for grain and timber.

choices.resultText:
“Grain and wood I have,” he says. “Wood especially.”

You did not pick that up when he said it.

He did not explain why he has so much wood, either.

Loading takes a while. He stands under the eaves and watches, and goes inside once in the middle of it. When he comes out there is a coat in his hand. Not for you. For the man driving.

“Put it all on the account,” he says. “We will settle up by and by.”

effects.logEntry: You asked for nothing at Millridge and rode back to Maplegate empty.

choices.resultText:
You stand up and say you have disturbed him.

For several seconds neither of you says anything.

He is waiting for you to finish. You have finished.

“Ah,” he says.

He stands as well, and the smile goes back on his face, and for the first time this evening it does not fit him.

“Well then,” he says. “Mind the road.”

He sees you to the study door. Half the lamps in the corridor are already out.

“About Maplegate,” he says as you are going out. “If you ever come round to it, any time.”

“I am not moving house.”

The wind on the ride home is stronger than it was coming out.

You brought nothing back. But the whole valley will know tomorrow that you went.
